Washington's New AI Laws and Your Business: What Takes Effect in 2027, and What Already Applies Today

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·13 min read·November 6, 2026

Your operations manager put a chatbot on the company website in the spring. Your HR platform added an AI screening feature to the applicant portal and nobody signed anything new for it. Someone in accounting has been pasting invoices into a free chatbot to summarize them. None of that was decided in a meeting, and none of it is unusual. Two Washington AI statutes were signed in March and take effect in 2027, and the useful question is narrower than the headlines suggest: most businesses will not be covered by either one, which leaves the law that was already on the books to govern all three of those things today.

This piece is for business owners, executives and in-house counsel rather than for lawyers advising other lawyers. I have written separately about what a law firm has to decide about its own AI use. What follows is the client-side version: what Washington actually enacted, who it reaches, and what to do about the AI already running inside your company.

What did Washington actually pass in 2026?

Two bills, both signed by Governor Ferguson on March 24, 2026, and neither in effect until 2027.

Engrossed Substitute House Bill 2225, chapter 168 of the 2026 Laws, regulates AI companion chatbots. It adds a new chapter to Title 19 RCW and takes effect January 1, 2027.

Engrossed Second Substitute House Bill 1170, chapter 167 of the 2026 Laws, requires provenance data in AI-generated images, audio and video, and separately requires public agencies to disclose when a consumer is interacting with an AI system. It takes effect February 1, 2027.

What matters more than either title is what the two statutes are not. Neither is a general AI law. Neither tells a Washington employer how to use AI in hiring, neither tells a clinic how to use an AI scribe, and neither sets out what a company owes anyone when a model gets something wrong. They are narrow statutes aimed at two specific products. Knowing that they are narrow is the first useful thing a business owner can learn here, because a good deal of what is being sold right now as AI compliance is sized for laws that Washington did not enact.

Does the companion chatbot law apply to my business?

Probably not, but the exemption is narrower than it first reads, and it is worth checking rather than assuming.

The statute reaches an "operator," defined as any person, partnership, corporation or entity that makes available or controls access to an AI companion chatbot for users in this state. There is no revenue threshold and no user-count threshold. A small company is an operator on the same terms as a large one.

The work is all done by the definition of the product. An AI companion chatbot is an AI system with a natural language interface that gives adaptive, human-like responses, including by exhibiting anthropomorphic features, and that is able to sustain a relationship across multiple interactions.

The business carve-out, and the sentence nobody has construed yet

The definition then excludes a bot used only for a business's operational purposes, productivity and analysis related to source information, internal research, technical assistance, or customer service, if that bot "does not sustain a relationship across multiple interactions and generate outputs that are likely to elicit emotional responses in the user."

Read that conditional closely, because it is doing a lot of work and it is ambiguous. It can be read as requiring both things before the exemption is lost, so that a bot which remembers a returning customer but says nothing emotionally resonant stays exempt. It can also be read as requiring a bot to do neither. No Washington court had construed it when this was written, and the statute does not take effect until January 1, 2027. If your customer service bot is deliberately designed to feel like a continuing relationship, which is what a good many of them are now marketed as, that sentence is the one that decides your exposure, and reading it the generous way is a choice rather than a conclusion.

There is a reason to think the ambiguity is real rather than invented. Two exclusions further down the same subsection use the identical pair of conditions, and the one covering a stand-alone voice assistant joins them with "or" rather than "and." The same drafter wrote both, in the same list, about the same two things.

Three other exclusions sit beside the business one, for a bot confined to a video game, a stand-alone voice assistant, and a narrowly tailored educational tool used in a school setting.

What an operator has to do

Give a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the chatbot is artificially generated and not human, at the beginning of the interaction and then at least every three hours of continued interaction. Take reasonable measures to stop the bot from claiming to be human, including when a user asks it directly, and from generating output that contradicts the disclosure.

An operator also may not make a companion chatbot available or deploy it at all unless it maintains and implements a protocol for detecting and addressing suicidal ideation and expressions of self-harm, including eating disorders. The protocol has to refer users to crisis resources such as a suicide hotline or crisis text line, and take reasonable measures against output encouraging or describing how to commit self-harm. Its details have to be published on the operator's website and inside the application, together with the number of crisis referral notifications issued in the preceding calendar year. That last one is a public reporting obligation, it applies to every operator rather than only to those with minor users, and it is the duty most likely to be missed.

Where the operator knows the user is a minor, or the chatbot is directed to minors, the duties go further. The notice interval drops from three hours to one. Sexually explicit and suggestive content has to be prevented. And the statute lists eight manipulative engagement techniques that have to be prohibited, running from mimicking a romantic bond to simulating distress when a user says they want to end the conversation.

Does the AI content provenance law apply to my business?

Almost certainly not, and there are two independent reasons rather than one.

The first is the threshold. HB 1170 reaches a "covered provider," which the statute defines as a person or entity that creates, codes, or otherwise produces a generative AI system that has over 1,000,000 monthly users and is publicly accessible within this state to consumers for personal use. That is written for the model developers, not for the companies that buy their products. The definition also excludes state, local and tribal governments outright.

The one place to look twice is the phrase "creates, codes, or otherwise produces." Nobody has construed "otherwise produces," and a company that fine-tunes or white-labels somebody else's model sits closer to that phrase than a company that simply buys a subscription.

The second reason does not depend on size at all. The act says nothing in the chapter may be construed to apply to business-to-business uses, sales, licensing or distribution of generative AI systems. A company selling an AI product to other companies stays outside the chapter however large it gets. The act separately excludes products providing exclusively video game or interactive experiences.

What the act does not cover at all

Two limits on subject matter matter as much as the threshold. The act defines generative artificial intelligence as technology used to generate images, audio or video, and the provenance duty runs to video, image and audio content. AI-written text is outside this chapter altogether. The chatbot on your website and the model summarizing your invoices are not what this statute is about.

Public agencies are in a different section, and a different title

A city, a county or a public agency should not stop at the covered-provider analysis, because that definition never reached it. A separate section of the same act, placed in a new chapter of Title 42 RCW rather than the Title 19 chapter that holds the rest, imposes an unrelated duty. A government agency that makes available an AI system intended to interact with consumers has to tell each consumer, before or at the time of the interaction, that they are dealing with an AI system. The disclosure has to be clear, conspicuously posted, in plain language, and free of dark patterns, and subsection (3) requires it whether or not a reasonable consumer would have worked it out anyway.

Why the difference in how the two laws are enforced is the part to notice

This is the detail that most summaries skip, and for a Washington business it is the one with teeth.

HB 1170 says expressly that only the attorney general can bring an action under the Consumer Protection Act pursuant to its enforcement section, and it gives the attorney general authority to sue in the name of the state or as parens patriae. The act creates no private right of action, so a private plaintiff has no route in under this chapter.

HB 2225 contains no such limit. It declares that the practices it covers vitally affect the public interest and that a violation is an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce and an unfair method of competition for purposes of chapter 19.86 RCW, and then stops. Chapter 19.86 is the Consumer Protection Act. RCW 19.86.090 gives a person injured in business or property by a violation of RCW 19.86.020, 19.86.030, 19.86.040, 19.86.050 or 19.86.060 a civil action in superior court to enjoin further violations, to recover actual damages, or both, together with the costs of suit including a reasonable attorney's fee. The court may in its discretion increase the award up to three times actual damages, and for a violation of RCW 19.86.020 that increased award may not exceed twenty-five thousand dollars.

So one statute is enforced by the attorney general alone and the other appears to leave a private action open. I say appears because the declaration supplies some of a Consumer Protection Act claim and not the whole of it. On its own words it establishes that the practices affect the public interest, that a violation is unfair or deceptive, that it occurs in trade or commerce, and that it is not reasonable in relation to the development and preservation of business. What it does not supply is injury to the plaintiff's own business or property, or causation, and those remain the plaintiff's to prove. But the practical shape is clear enough, and the fee provision rather than the damages cap is what makes a small claim worth bringing.

What law already governs how my company uses AI?

All of it. This is the point that gets lost whenever a new statute is announced.

The Consumer Protection Act already reaches a deceptive statement about your product whether a person or a model wrote it. Your contracts already allocate who is responsible for an error, and most of them were signed before anyone involved was thinking about AI. Negligence law does not have a software exception. The confidentiality obligations you owe under customer agreements, under sector rules, and under your own privacy policy apply to the data your staff paste into a chatbot, and they applied the day before anyone pasted anything.

Nothing about using a new tool suspends an existing duty. The exposure in most companies right now is not a 2027 statute. It is a 2023 contract and an undocumented habit.

If this is describing your situation, tell me what is going on. I read what comes in myself, and I will tell you whether it is something I can help with.

Tell me about your situation

AI in hiring is an employment problem before it is an AI problem

Washington's Law Against Discrimination, chapter 49.60 RCW, governs employment decisions in this state, and it does not care what tool produced the decision. If a screening tool filters out applicants in a way that correlates with a protected characteristic, the employer made that decision. The vendor built the filter. The employer applied it.

Two practical consequences follow. The first is that you need to know what the tool actually scores, and a surprising number of employers do not, because the vendor treats it as proprietary and nobody asked before signing. The second is that you need to be able to reconstruct what happened to a particular applicant months later, which is a records question that most AI hiring deployments do not answer on their own.

If you hire in more than one state, the analysis widens. Other jurisdictions have begun regulating automated employment decisions directly, and the rules that reach you may turn on where the applicant sits rather than on where your office is. Neither question has a general answer, and both are worth checking against the specific states you hire in rather than assuming.

What should be in the contract with an AI vendor?

The sales page is not the agreement, and the agreement is usually where the interesting silence lives. Five things are worth finding before you sign.

Whether your data trains the model, and whether that answer changes between the free tier, the paid tier and the enterprise tier of the same product. It commonly does.

Who owns the output, and what the vendor warrants about it. Many agreements assign you the output and warrant nothing about whether it infringes anything.

What happens when the model changes. The thing you validated in March may not be the thing answering in September, and most agreements reserve that right without notice.

Indemnity, and whether it is capped at the fees you paid. An indemnity capped at a monthly subscription is not risk transfer. It is a refund.

Whether you can audit, or at least get a straight answer in writing, when something goes wrong and a customer or a regulator is asking.

What should a business actually write down?

Less than the vendors selling governance platforms will tell you, and more than nothing, which is where most companies are.

A usable policy fits on two pages and answers five questions. Which tools are approved. What information may never be put into one, named concretely rather than as a category. Who approves a new tool before anyone uses it. What has to be checked by a person before AI output goes to a customer, into a filing, or into a decision about an employee. And who gets told when it goes wrong.

The value is not in the document. It is in having made the decision once, in advance, rather than in the middle of an incident when the answer gets decided by whoever happens to be in the room.

Where this goes wrong

A free chatbot account with customer data in it, opened by a well-meaning employee, outside any agreement the company negotiated and outside any retention policy it has.

Buying an AI compliance program sized for a law that does not apply to you, while the actual exposure sits unread in a vendor agreement.

Assuming the vendor's indemnity covers you, without reading what it is capped at.

Treating a hiring tool as a technology purchase, so it never goes past IT and procurement and nobody with employment responsibility sees what it screens on.

Writing a policy, circulating it once, and never building any way to find out whether anyone follows it.

Waiting for 2027. Both statutes take effect then, and neither of them is what is likely to cause your first problem.

What a lawyer does here

Works out which rules actually reach your company, and says so plainly.

Reads the agreements you already signed and tells you what they permit in the gaps, rather than what the sales page said.

Writes the policy to the size of the business, and builds the approval step into something people will actually do.

Looks at the AI already running in the company, which is almost always more than the executive team believes, and sorts it by what it touches rather than by what it costs.

Works through it with you when something goes wrong, when the question becomes not only what the policy said but what you can show about what you actually did.
